summary: Taskset published a concentrated run of early Commodore games, particularly on the Commodore 64, with arcade-style releases such as Pipeline, Super Pipeline and Bozo's Night Out.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Taskset Commodore releases including Cosmic Convoy, Pipeline, Gyropod, Bozo's Night Out and Super Pipeline II.
The museum records recurring contributors including Andy Walker and Paul Hodgson across several Taskset games.
note: The surviving institutional record is catalogue-focused, so this profile avoids unsupported claims about Taskset's ownership or founders.

summary: Team17 was formed in 1990 from people associated with 17-Bit Software and Team 7 and quickly became strongly identified with the Commodore Amiga as both a developer and publisher.
facts: Team17's official history states that the company was founded on 7 December 1990 by Debbie Bestwick, Martyn Brown and Michael Robinson when 17-Bit Software and Team 7 came together.
Its first game was Full Contact for the Commodore Amiga in 1991, followed by Alien Breed, which developed into a major Team17 series.
Team17's own retrospective describes the company's early vision as making games for the Commodore Amiga.
note: The historical facts are taken from Team17's own company history and retrospective material.

summary: Terminal Software published a small but concentrated group of early Commodore 64 games during 1983 and 1984, including Super Gridder, Super Dogfight and Plumb Crazy.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves six Commodore 64 games under the Terminal Software publishing credit.
The museum records releases from 1983 and 1984 including Hunter, Stellar Dodger, Super Gridder, Super Dogfight, Plumb Crazy and Triple Tournament.
note: Reliable company-level documentation is limited, so the profile sticks to the preserved software record.

summary: The Edge published British home-computer games through the mid-to-late 1980s, with a catalogue spanning original titles, licensed characters and arcade-related releases across several 8-bit formats.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Commodore 64 releases under The Edge including Wizardry, Quo Vadis and Garfield: Winter's Tail.
Its wider Spectrum catalogue includes Fairlight, Bobby Bearing, Shadow Skimmer and licensed Garfield software.
note: Some Edge releases carried joint or licensed publishing relationships, so CCG retains version-specific credits on game pages.

summary: Titus published games across 8-bit and 16-bit computers during the late 1980s and early 1990s, with Commodore releases ranging from driving and action titles to Amiga games such as The Blues Brothers.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Titus releases on Commodore, Amstrad, Spectrum and PC systems.
Its Commodore records include Crazy Cars, Wild Streets, Battle Storm and The Blues Brothers.
note: The museum catalogue supports Titus's multi-format publishing activity; this profile avoids unsupported corporate-history detail.

summary: Tynesoft built a broad British home-computer catalogue across the 1980s, publishing games on the BBC Micro, Acorn Electron, Commodore systems, ZX Spectrum and other platforms.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves seventy-eight game records under the Tynesoft publishing credit.
The museum collection spans numerous 8-bit platforms and includes sports, licensed and arcade-style games, with Commodore releases extending across the C16/Plus 4 and Commodore 64.
note: The museum's broad catalogue provides strong evidence for Tynesoft's multi-format publishing activity without requiring speculative company-history claims.

summary: Ultimate Play The Game was the publishing name of Ashby Computers and Graphics Ltd., formed in 1982 by brothers Tim and Chris Stamper. The label became one of the best-known British 8-bit game names of the early-to-mid 1980s.
facts: The Centre for Computing History records Ultimate Play The Game as the publishing name of Ashby Computers and Graphics Ltd., formed in 1982 by Tim and Chris Stamper.
The museum identifies Jetpac and Pssst as the company's first two releases in 1983.
Its Commodore collection records Ultimate titles including The Staff of Karnath, Entombed, Underwurlde and Outlaws.
note: Ultimate's C64 catalogue includes both conversions and games created externally for the platform, so developer credits remain separate.

summary: Virgin Mastertronic was the later form of the Mastertronic business after Virgin became involved. It combined software publishing with a major role in Sega distribution before the business was reorganised in the early 1990s.
facts: Anthony Guter's first-person Mastertronic history records that the company later became Virgin Mastertronic.
Guter states that the business became the exclusive UK supplier for Sega consoles and software.
He records that by 1992 Virgin disposed of the Sega distribution side and the remaining games businesses were reorganised as Virgin Interactive Entertainment.
note: The historical account comes from former Mastertronic financial controller and systems manager Anthony Guter.

summary: Zeppelin Games published budget and mid-price computer games from the late 1980s into the early 1990s, with releases spread across the Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari 8-bit, Spectrum and Amstrad systems.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves sixteen game records under the Zeppelin Games publishing credit.
The museum catalogue includes Commodore releases such as International Tennis, World Soccer and Jocky Wilson's Dart Challenge, as well as later Amiga software.
note: The institutional record is strongest for Zeppelin's software catalogue, so the profile stays focused on documented publishing activity.
